defects.claim: Model C / 'uncertain' list: the defence that a fixed, pre-announced, operator-funded prize is not a 'wagering pool ... conducted for profit' under 26 U.S.C. § 4421(1)(B) is 'untested', and 'I found no ruling, case or IRS guidance testing it. AM 2020-009 involved entrant-funded DFS pools and does not resolve it.'
defects.correction: This is refuted by the very memo the brief cites. I extracted the full text of AM 2020-009 (POSTS-104958-20, dated 23 July 2020, released 8/7/2020). It discusses Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779 at length — a PUZZLE CONTEST with entry fees and guaranteed payments to winners. The memo states the ruling held that 'contesting for a prize offered by another in a contest of mental or physical skill of the contestant, which the one offering the prize must award in any event, is not gaming; and, the fact that each contestant is required to pay an entrance fee does not make the payment a bet or gaming transaction unless the entrance fees alone comprise the prize.' It adds: 'the operator has obligated itself to pay a sum certain in prizes which is not contingent on the number or amount of entrance fees. The ruling concluded that the puzzle game was not a wagering pool or lottery within the meaning of IRC § 4421.' Rev. Rul. 57-521 is the single most favourable authority in existence for Model C's excise-tax position, it is directly on point for a knowledge contest with an operator-funded fixed prize, and the brief omits it entirely while asserting no such authority exists.

defects.claim: Headline and risks: the federal wagering excise tax is a gate 'which the IRS has already applied to paid-entry skill contests regardless of skill-vs-chance'; Model C: AM 2020-009 reasoned 'expressly that skill-vs-chance is irrelevant for federal excise purposes'; '§ 4421 draws no skill/chance distinction at all.'
defects.correction: AM 2020-009 says the statutory language 'does not differentiate whether an activity involves skill, chance, or some combination of the two' — but the very next sentence reads: 'Still, the presence or absence of skill in a contest may help determine whether an entry fee constitutes a taxable wager, or not.' The memo then expressly distinguishes a pure-skill contest from DFS: 'In the revenue ruling, the contest participant's own skill was the only factor involved in winning the puzzle game and there was no chance element at all. In contrast, DFS participants merely select a lineup ... and have no ability to exercise control or influence over the actions of the players.' The IRS applied the tax to DFS, not to 'paid-entry skill contests' generally, and its stated reason was precisely that the DFS entrant does NOT control the outcome. A trivia duel, where the entrant's own knowledge determines the result, sits on the Rev. Rul. 57-521 side of the line the memo draws. The brief inverts the memo's reasoning and presents excise tax as 'the under-appreciated killer' when the cited authority is materially favourable.

defects.claim: Model B: a § 5363 violation exposes the operator 'to fine, up to 5 years and a permanent injunction under § 5366'.
defects.correction: Injunctive relief is 31 U.S.C. § 5365, not § 5366. I confirmed § 5365 ('Civil remedies') gives district courts 'original and exclusive jurisdiction to prevent and restrain restricted transactions', authorises a TRO, preliminary injunction or injunction under FRCP 65, and vests standing in the Attorney General, State attorneys general and specified tribal authorities. § 5366 is the criminal-penalties section (fine and/or up to 5 years) only and contains no injunction authority. The brief folds a remedy from one section into another.

defects.claim: Model D: the 2024 amended Negative Option Rule 'was VACATED IN ITS ENTIRETY by the Eighth Circuit in July 2025 ... There is therefore currently NO FTC negative option rule.' Checklist repeats 'so there is currently no rule.'
defects.correction: The Eighth Circuit vacated the 2024 RULE (the amendments creating the click-to-cancel regime), which restored the pre-existing 1973 Negative Option Rule — the Prenotification Negative Option Plan rule still codified at 16 C.F.R. Part 425. The FTC's own restarted rulemaking confirms this: per Gibson Dunn's account of the ANPRM (submitted to OIRA 30 Jan 2026, published 11 March 2026, comments due 13 April 2026), it asks 'whether the agency should amend the EXISTING Negative Option Rule' and 'certain provisions of the vacated Click-to-Cancel Rule' — two distinct instruments. Saying there is 'NO FTC negative option rule' is wrong; the correct statement is that there is currently no click-to-cancel rule, while the narrower 1973 rule remains on the books. The brief also gives the OIRA submission date as if it were the ANPRM date and omits the 11 March 2026 publication.

defects.claim: Model C: 'If you hold a withdrawable cash balance for users, or the pool is entrant-funded, FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7 pulls you back toward money transmitter status.' Checklist: 'Trigger analysis rests on FinCEN Guidance FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7.'
defects.correction: I extracted the guidance. Section 4.7 is titled 'CVC Money Transmission Performed by Internet Casinos' and its operative sentence is limited to a person who 'accepts and transmits value denominated in CVC'. The whole of FIN-2019-G001 is guidance on convertible virtual currency. A dollar-denominated withdrawable user balance is plain 'funds', not CVC, so § 4.7 is not the governing authority for that fact pattern — 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A) is. Resting the Model C trigger analysis on a CVC guidance section is a category error that would misdirect the counsel opinion the checklist tells the founder to commission. (The § 4.7 quotation is also truncated: the actual text ends 'at the moment the condition is satisfied AND THE ACCEPTANCE OR TRANSMISSION TAKES PLACE' — the brief closes the quotation mark after 'satisfied', dropping a clause that matters to whether a duel escrow is transmission at all.)

defects.claim: Headline: Skillz v. Papaya is listed under the federal gate '(3) FTC Act § 5 / COPPA' and called 'the single most dangerous precedent'; the judgment is described as '$719m'.
defects.correction: Three problems. (a) Jurisdiction of claim: I confirmed via the law-firm analysis the brief itself cites that this was a competitor suit under the Lanham Act and New York General Business Law. FTC Act § 5 has no private right of action and the FTC was not a party; filing it under an 'FTC Act § 5 / COPPA' heading misdescribes the source of the exposure. The brief's own Model C text gets this right, so the headline contradicts the body. (b) 'Precedent': this is an S.D.N.Y. district-court judgment entered 28 July 2026, subject to appeal to the Second Circuit. It binds no one and is not precedent anywhere; the brief nowhere notes that appeal rights exist or that the judgment is not final. (c) Amount: the source states the court 'separately awarded $719 million in disgorgement — an ALTERNATIVE REMEDY THE PLAINTIFF MAY ELECT IN LIEU OF DAMAGES' following an April jury verdict of $420m. The headline's bare '$719m' and the checklist's '$719m disgorgement plus $10.1m fees' read as a cumulative total; they are alternative, not additive.

defects.claim: Model A authority line cites '31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(A) and (1)(E)(viii)' as support for the lawfulness of purchased closed-loop cosmetic coins.
defects.correction: I confirmed the text of (1)(E)(viii): it covers participation where participants 'do not stake or risk anything of value other than — (I) personal efforts ... or (II) points or credits that the sponsor of the game or contest provides to participants FREE OF CHARGE'. Model A coins are bought for dollars, so (viii) does not apply to them. The brief's own risks section says exactly this ('That exclusion is written around free credits. It stops applying the moment coins are sold for money'), so the authority line contradicts the analysis. Model A's real argument is the (1)(A) 'no prize of value' point; the (viii) cite should be removed or confined to the existing free-coin demo.

defects.claim: 'FinCEN Prepaid Access Final Rule, 76 FR 45403, 26 July 2011'.
defects.correction: The Federal Register publication is 76 FR 45403–45420, Vol. 76 No. 146, FRIDAY 29 JULY 2011 (confirmed on govinfo). 26 July 2011 is the date of FinCEN's press release announcing the rule — which is in fact the document sitting at the URL the brief lists in its own sources (fincen.gov/system/files/shared/20110726b.pdf is a two-page press release, not the rule). A citation pairing the FR page with the press-release date will not check out. The substantive threshold is right: 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(4)(iii) excludes an arrangement that 'provides closed loop prepaid access to funds not to exceed $2,000 maximum value that can be associated with a prepaid access device or vehicle on any day.'

defects.claim: 'Louisiana 1 Aug 2026' in the list of state dual-currency/sweepstakes bans.
defects.correction: The Louisiana sweepstakes measure is SB 181 of the 2025 Regular Session, whose bill notation on the legislature's own page is '(8/1/25)' — 1 August 2025, not 2026. The docket I retrieved also shows a 12 June 2025 veto message, so both the date AND whether the ban is in force at all need checking against the primary source. Given a founder would use these dates to sequence a geo-block, a year-off date is operationally material even though the brief flags state material as secondary-sourced.

defects.claim: 'Indiana HB 1052 eff. 1 Jul 2026'; and 'the FAIR BET Act and FULL HOUSE Act (S.2230 / H.R.6985) would repeal it'.
defects.correction: I could not confirm either bill number. Indiana's legislative page for HB 1052 (2026) returned no matching subject matter. For the wagering-loss repeal bills, congress.gov and govtrack both blocked retrieval, but the FAIR BET Act is commonly reported as H.R. 4304 (119th Cong., Rep. Titus), not H.R. 6985; S. 2230 for the FULL HOUSE Act is plausible but unverified. Treat both bill numbers as unverified rather than citable — the brief presents them without the UNVERIFIED marker it correctly applies elsewhere.

missing: Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779 — the operator-funded, fixed-prize skill-contest ruling discussed inside AM 2020-009 itself. It is the strongest authority available for Model C's excise-tax position and for the proposition that an entry fee in a contest of mental skill is not a wager unless the entry fees alone comprise the prize. Its absence is what makes the brief's excise-tax risk framing wrong in direction, not just in degree.

Marchetti v. United States, 390 U.S. 39 (1968) and Grosso v. United States — the Fifth Amendment self-incrimination problem with §§ 4411/4412 registration. The checklist tells the founder to file Form 11-C 'before accepting any wagers' at the $500 unauthorised rate. Registering at the unauthorised rate is a public admission of accepting wagers not authorised under state law, i.e. potential evidence of a § 1955 / state gambling offence. This interaction needs a caveat before anyone files; verify the current scope of the privilege with counsel.

That the Papaya judgment is subject to appeal and is not final. The brief calls it 'precedent' and builds a checklist item and a headline gate on it without noting that a district-court judgment entered six weeks before the brief's date will almost certainly be appealed, and binds no court.

The 1973 Prenotification Negative Option Rule survived the Eighth Circuit vacatur and remains at 16 C.F.R. Part 425. A founder told 'there is currently NO FTC negative option rule' may skip checking whether their offer is a prenotification plan.

Scope of the FTC's 25 February 2026 'Enforcement Policy Statement Promoting the Adoption of Age-Verification Technology' (confirmed to exist). The brief asserts it 'gives limited relief for data collected solely to run age-verification technology' but does not state its conditions — and a money model that hard-blocks under-18s will be relying on exactly that collection.

State automatic-renewal laws (California's ARL, New York, and others) for Model D. The brief verdicts Model D 'lawful' on the federal layer and then tells the founder to build to click-to-cancel standards 'anyway' for prudential reasons — when several states impose click-to-cancel-equivalent obligations as binding law, not prudence.

31 U.S.C. § 5363's predicate that the defendant be 'engaged in the business of betting or wagering', and the § 1084(b) safe harbour. Both are threshold elements the brief's Model B liability analysis assumes away.

State money transmitter licensing appears only in the risks narrative, never as a checklist item, even though the brief itself calls it 'the real cost driver for Models B and C'. A founder working the checklist top-to-bottom will not see it as an action.

defects.claim: N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(1) defines 'something of value' to include 'extension of a service, entertainment or a privilege of playing at a game or scheme without charge' — cited four times (Model A reasoning, Model A authority, New York subdivision, checklist item on purchased coins), and separately 'the material-element test at Penal Law s.225.00(2)'.
defects.correction: Both subsection numbers are wrong, and they are effectively swapped. Per the official text at nysenate.gov: s.225.00(1) is 'Contest of chance' — 'any contest, game, gaming scheme or gaming device in which the outcome depends in a material degree upon an element of chance' (i.e. the material-element test the brief assigns to (2)). s.225.00(2) is 'Gambling'. The 'something of value' definition the brief quotes, with the 'extension of a service, entertainment or a privilege of playing at a game or scheme without charge' language, is s.225.00(6). The quoted language is genuine and the substantive NY analysis survives, but every cite to it must be renumbered to s.225.00(6), and the material-degree cite to s.225.00(1).

defects.claim: 'Montana Code Ann. s.23-5-110 defines a lawful contest of skill as one where the contestant is not required to pay anything of value ... to participate' — relied on five times (headline skill-wagering list, Model B, Model C, Model C authority, Montana subdivision) to make Montana an 'absolute geofence' with 'TWO INDEPENDENT PROHIBITIONS'.
defects.correction: MCA 23-5-110 is titled 'Public policy of state concerning gambling' and is a legislative-findings section — it contains no definition of 'contest of skill' and no paid-entry disqualifier. Montana's definitions section is 23-5-112, which defines gambling as 'risking any money ... for a gain that is contingent in whole or in part upon lot, chance, or the operation of a gambling device or gambling enterprise' — a chance-based definition that cuts against, not for, the brief's claim, and which per the same source contains no 'contest of skill' definition either. Montana's inclusion in the headline list of states that 'criminalise wagering on contests of SKILL by statute' rests entirely on this bad cite and should be dropped pending a real citation. Montana's genuine exposure is S.B. 555 (dual-currency sweepstakes), not a skill-wagering statute.

defects.claim: Headline and checklist: 'twelve more enacted express dual-currency "online sweepstakes" bans in 2025-26 ... (CA, CT, IN, IA, LA, ME, MT, NV, NJ, NY, OK, TN)'.
defects.correction: The count is contradicted by the brief's own subdivision entries. Iowa: the brief itself says S.F. 2289 'does NOT define dual-currency systems or create a new criminal offence — it is a broad enforcement grant'. Nevada: the brief itself says S.B. 256 'added enforcement tools against unlicensed online operators'. Neither is an express dual-currency ban. The defensible statement is roughly ten express dual-currency bans plus two enforcement-authority grants; the brief should not present the two as equivalent, because the compliance question in IA and NV turns on regulator discretion rather than on a statutory dual-currency definition the founder can read against the product.

defects.claim: 'As of Sep 2026, 31 states have enacted the CSBS MTMA in whole or in part; Massachusetts became the 26th adopter effective 1 Jan 2026 and Virginia's version takes effect 1 Jul 2026.'
defects.correction: Internally inconsistent — 31 enacted states and Massachusetts as the 26th adopter cannot both be right in the same sentence, and the brief gives no basis for either figure. One of the two numbers is wrong. Treat the MTMA adopter count as unverified; the operative conclusion ('plan for 49 applications, not one') does not depend on it and should be stated without the false precision.

defects.claim: 'Verified live statutes: ... Kentucky KRS 372.020 (losses of $5+ recoverable; if the loser does not sue within six months, ANY OTHER PERSON may sue for TREBLE the loss)' — repeated in the Kentucky subdivision as the 'highest private-litigation risk in the United States'.
defects.correction: The six-month / 'any other person' / treble-damages mechanism is KRS 372.040, not KRS 372.020. KRS 372.020 is the loser's own action to recover the amount lost. The brief labels this a 'verified live statute', which it is — but the cite packs two sections into one number. Splitting them matters because the treble/any-person standing in 372.040 is the provision that actually creates the outsized exposure the brief is warning about.

defects.claim: White v. Cuomo, 38 N.Y.3d 209 (2022) is 'THE BEST AUTHORITY IN THE COUNTRY' for Model C, a '4-3' decision whose holding sentence is 'a design instruction' — 'Build to that sentence.'
defects.correction: Presented without its controlling limitation. White v. Cuomo was a holding on Article I, s.9 of the NEW YORK CONSTITUTION, about interactive fantasy sports that the legislature had affirmatively authorized in Racing Law art. 14 AND expressly exempted from Penal Law article 225. It does not hold that an unauthorized paid-entry trivia contest escapes Penal Law s.225.00's material-degree contest-of-chance test, and it has no precedential force outside New York. A founder told to 'build to that sentence' could conclude NY is cleared by design compliance alone; it is not. Separately, the '4-3' vote split is unverified (Justia, leagle, FindLaw and the NY Courts reporter were all unreachable) — do not state it without checking the opinion.

defects.claim: 'NO STATE LICENSES THIS. Peer-to-peer wagering on a mobile trivia app fits no existing state licence category ... so "lawful-only-with-licence" is not available as an answer' / 'no state issues a licence for peer-to-peer trivia wagering — so there is no licensed path'.
defects.correction: Stated as a categorical 51-jurisdiction absolute, and contradicted by the brief's own Nevada entry. NRS 463.0152 defines a 'gambling game' broadly as any game played 'for money ... or any representative of value' with no skill/chance distinction, and NRS 463.160 licenses exactly that — the brief itself says 'Any game that lets a player walk away with real value is a gambling game requiring a full Nevada gaming licence.' That is a licensed path, just a prohibitively expensive one. New Jersey's DGE likewise licenses esports event wagering. The accurate claim is that no state has an off-the-shelf licence category that fits at commercially viable cost and lead time — not that licensure is unavailable in principle.

defects.claim: 'Decide whether you will HOLD player funds at all. If yes, you need state money transmitter licences in 49 states plus DC.'
defects.correction: Stated as an automatic consequence of holding player funds, with no threshold question. Most state MTL regimes — and the MTMA definition the brief elsewhere relies on — turn on receiving money for TRANSMISSION TO ANOTHER PERSON. An operator that takes deposits and pays out its own prize obligations from its own funds (which is precisely Model C: operator-funded, fixed, entrant-count-independent prizes) is frequently not transmitting to a third party and may fall outside the definition entirely in many states. Model B, where the operator holds one player's stake for payment to another player, is the structure that squarely raises it. Collapsing the two into a flat '49 states plus DC' requirement materially overstates the burden for the very design the brief recommends, and the checklist calls it 'the single largest cost and time line item in the whole plan' on that basis.

defects.claim: 'Hawaii registration and bond for entry-fee contests with prizes of $5,000 or more' (checklist), repeated in the Hawaii subdivision.
defects.correction: The brief concedes this comes only from promotions-law compliance guides and 'not from a primary statute I read'. No Hawaii prize-promotion registration statute is identifiable, and the claim sits oddly next to the brief's own (correct) observation that Hawaii permits no legal gambling of any kind and has no gaming regulator — there is no agency to register with. Offering a registration route in Hawaii risks a founder treating paid entry there as curable by filing. It is not; the brief's own advice to geofence Hawaii is the right answer and the registration line should be struck.

defects.claim: Four 2026 enactments stated with precise signing dates and effect dates: Indiana H.B. 1052 / P.L. 153-2026 (signed 12 Mar 2026, eff. 1 Jul 2026); Iowa S.F. 2289 (signed 15 May 2026, eff. 1 Jul 2026); Maine L.D. 2007 (signed 6 Apr 2026, eff. mid-to-late Jul 2026); Tennessee S.B. 2136 (signed 22 May 2026, immediate). Also New Jersey A5447 'signed 15 Aug 2025'.
defects.correction: Unverified. I could not confirm any of these five from a primary legislative source (Indiana IGA, Iowa BillBook, NJ Legislature and legiscan were blocked, JS-rendered or returned nothing). NJ A5447's TEXT is confirmed to exist and to target dual-currency sweepstakes with civil penalties of $100,000 first offence / $250,000 subsequent, but its enactment and the 15 Aug 2025 signing date are not confirmed. Note this is a flag for verification, not an accusation of fabrication: every 2025-26 enactment I COULD reach checked out exactly — CA AB 831 (signed 11 Oct 2025, Ch. 623, adds Penal Code s.337o), NY S5935A (signed 5 Dec 2025, Ch. 605, adds Rac. Pari-Mut. Wag. & Breeding L. s.912, $10,000-$100,000 per violation), and OK S.B. 1589 (vetoed 7 May 2026, overridden 14 May 2026, Class C2 felony, eff. 1 Nov 2026, with the dual-currency 'representative of value' definition and geolocation/platform/media-affiliate liability all verbatim as described). Confirm the remaining five before relying on the specific dates in a launch timeline.

missing: Tribal gaming compacts. The brief never mentions them. Exclusivity provisions in California, Florida, Oklahoma, Connecticut and elsewhere give tribes independent standing and enforcement leverage against unlicensed real-money gaming, and tribal objection has killed products that had a clean reading of the criminal code. This is a state-layer risk that sits alongside, not inside, the statutes analysed.

Unclaimed property / escheat on unredeemed coin balances. Model A and Model D both accumulate stored value. Several states treat unredeemed prepaid balances as abandoned property with reporting and remittance duties. This is a live state-layer obligation for the two models the brief clears as 'lawful' with no caveat beyond in-app purchase disclosure.

Age of majority is not 18 everywhere. The checklist prescribes a flat '18+' gate. Alabama and Nebraska set majority at 19 and Mississippi at 21, which affects both contract enforceability (including the arbitration clause the brief tells the founder to build) and the minors' in-app-purchase exposure it identifies as the most common enforcement hook.

Player-side versus operator-side liability is only disentangled for Illinois. Several of the skill-wagering statutes the brief relies on — 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) and Cal. Penal Code s.337a among them — reach the person who plays or bets, not just the house. A founder needs to know whether geofencing protects the company, the user, or both, because the answer drives the terms of service and the refund posture.

No state-law analysis of the free-entry ('AMOE') alternative. The brief jumps from Model B to Model C without evaluating whether a genuine alternative method of entry would remove the consideration element and open more states. That is the standard structure the sweepstakes industry actually uses, and the 2025-26 bans the brief catalogues are precisely a legislative response to it — so its omission leaves the strategy space incompletely mapped.

Effective-date sequencing for the geofence. The checklist lists in-force dates ranging from 5 Dec 2025 to 1 Nov 2026 but never says what a founder launching before 1 Nov 2026 should do about Oklahoma, or whether geofencing can be staged. Given that today is 14 Sep 2026, OK (1 Nov 2026) is the only listed ban not yet operative, and the brief does not surface that.

defects.claim: AMLR 'Art. 20(5) requires CDD upon the collection of winnings, the wagering of a stake, or both, at €2,000 or more' (checklist, AMLR item; repeated in risks).
defects.correction: The provision is Article 19(5) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, not Article 20(5). Verified from the consolidated OJ text: Article 19 'Application of customer due diligence measures', paragraph 5 — 'providers of gambling services shall apply customer due diligence measures upon the collection of winnings, the wagering of a stake, or both, when carrying out transactions amounting to at least EUR 2 000'. Article 20 is the article listing the CDD *measures* themselves (Art. 19(5) cross-refers to 'Article 20(1), point (a)'). The brief labels this item 'VERIFIED PRIMARY TEXT', which makes the wrong article number worse, not better.

defects.claim: AMLR Art. 4 'lets member states exempt low-risk gambling services, BUT the exemption shall not apply to... providers of gambling services the principal activity of which is to provide online gambling services or sport betting services. Translation: FACT//DUEL under Model B or C cannot be exempted.'
defects.correction: The brief truncates Article 4(1) mid-sentence. The actual text continues: '...or sport betting services, **other than: (i) online gambling services operated by the State... (ii) online gambling services the organisation, operation and administration of which is regulated by the State.**' Recital 63 confirms the carve-back. The omitted words are the operative ones: an operator inside a state-regulated online regime is not automatically outside the exemption. The brief also omits that Art. 4 exemptions require a Member State risk assessment and (per recital 63) Commission approval/rejection, so 'cannot be exempted' is stated far more flatly than the text supports.

defects.claim: 'THE EU HAS NOW WRITTEN SKILL IS NOT AN ESCAPE INTO DIRECTLY APPLICABLE LAW... From 10 July 2027 a Model B or Model C FACT//DUEL is an obliged entity with full CDD at a €2,000 threshold.'
defects.correction: Art. 2(1)(12) AMLR (verified text) defines a gambling service as one 'which involves wagering a stake with monetary value in **games of chance**, including those with an element of skill'. The chance limb is still required; 'including those with an element of skill' extends the definition to mixed games, it does not abolish it for skill-predominant ones. A Model C contest that genuinely has no chance element — which is the entire basis of the brief's own German/Austrian/Dutch Camp 1 analysis — is arguably not a 'game of chance' and so arguably not an AMLR gambling service at all. The brief asserts AMLR capture of Model C as settled; it is not, and the brief's two positions (Model C is chance-free enough to escape §3(1) GlüStV, but is an AMLR game of chance) cannot both be safely assumed.

defects.claim: 'Malta is the only EU state with a purpose-built skill-games regime: the Skill Games Regulations (S.L. 438.11), in force 24 January 2017...' — cited as current authority in the Model C reasoning, the Malta subdivision and the authority lines.
defects.correction: legislation.mt records S.L. 438.11 (Skill Games Regulations) as **repealed by Act XVI of 2018** — the Gaming Act (Cap. 583), which replaced the Lotteries and Other Games Act (Cap. 438) and its subsidiary legislation. Presenting a repealed 2017 instrument as the live Maltese skill-games regime, nine years after repeal, is a material citation failure. The current instruments are the Gaming Act Cap. 583 and its subsidiary legislation — the MGA's own regulatory-framework page lists S.L. 583.3–583.12 (Gaming Authorisations Regulations are S.L. 583.5, not 438.11). The substantive controlled-skill-game concept does survive under Cap. 583 and MGA Directive 6 of 2018 (which does exist and is titled 'Controlled Skill Games Ruling' — that part checks out), but the statutory citation does not.

defects.claim: Sweden is in 'Camp 1 — outside gambling law, no licence' for Model C (headline: 'outside gambling law in DE/AT/NL/SE'), on the strength of a Spelinspektionen page about competitions decided by a 'prestationsmoment'.
defects.correction: Spellagen (2018:1138) defines **kombinationsspel** — 'a game where the participant may win a prize and the chance of winning depends on a combination of skill and chance' — as a licensable form of spel, structurally identical to the Danish kombinationsspil the brief treats as fatal. The brief mentions kombinationsspel only for Denmark and never tells the reader Sweden has the same concept, while simultaneously conceding (in the Sweden subdivision and the risks) that a randomly drawn question set introduces 'inslag av slump'. On its own facts, FACT//DUEL's paid duel is a candidate Swedish kombinationsspel requiring a Spelinspektionen licence. The brief's own subdivision entry marks Sweden 'licence-required', directly contradicting the headline and Camp 1 — a founder reading the headline would launch paid contests in Sweden unlicensed.

defects.claim: 'Germany's GGL issues permissions only for sports betting (§ 21), online poker (§ 22b), virtual slot machines (§ 22a), lotteries and horse betting... so it is not merely unlicensed but unlicensable.'
defects.correction: The GGL's own legal-basis page (which the brief cites as a source) states that GlüStV 2021 made licensable 'virtuelle Automatenspiele, Online-Poker **und Onlinecasinospiele**' — online casino games are a permission class the brief's 'exhaustive' list omits entirely. It also conflates regulators: online casino games are authorised by the individual Länder (several run their own concession procedures), not by the GGL, which handles sports betting, virtual slots and online poker. The enumeration being incomplete undercuts the categorical 'unlicensable' verdict, which is the brief's whole basis for 'drop Model B in Germany' rather than 'restructure and apply'.

defects.claim: 'Model C (fixed announced prize pool, entry fee, skill-determined) falls outside § 3(1) GlüStV entirely if chance does not predominate — no permission needed.'
defects.correction: Falling outside § 3(1) GlüStV does not mean no German permission is needed. § 33d GewO requires a permit (Erlaubnis) for the commercial operation of 'andere Spiele mit Gewinnmöglichkeit' — other games offering a chance to win that are *not* Glücksspiel — precisely the category a paid skill contest lands in when it escapes the GlüStV. Its application to purely online offerings is contested, which is exactly why it belongs in the brief. The brief never mentions §§ 33d/33h GewO anywhere, and its advice line is 'run Model C in Germany unlicensed on the skill-predominance analysis'. That is the single most consequential omission in the document, since Germany is the market the brief tells the founder to launch in first.

defects.claim: 'The CJEU confirmed in Case C-440/23 that an operator licensed in one member state has no right to serve players in a member state that prohibits the product, and that players there can recover their losses (judgment reported 16 April 2026; AG Emiliou opinion 4 September 2025).' Relied on in three separate places.
defects.correction: I could not confirm this case exists in the form described. curia.europa.eu returns no retrievable record for C-440/23, and the Commission's own gambling case-law page (a brief source) lists no case after Sporting Odds (C-3/17, 28 February 2018) and does not mention C-440/23. The brief self-flags the date and holdings as secondary-sourced, but then builds a headline risk on it — 'Serving Germany, the Netherlands or Austria on a Malta licence creates a restitution liability equal to gross player losses' — stated as established law. Treat the case number, the 16 April 2026 judgment date, the AG Emiliou attribution and the three-limb holding as unverified until checked on curia.europa.eu. The underlying no-mutual-recognition principle is sound on older authority (Schindler, Läärä, Zenatti, Placanica); the specific 2026 case is not.

defects.claim: 'Gaming tax on Maltese-located players: 10% for Types 2, 3 and 4 and 15% for Type 1 from 1 October 2026 (was 5%)' via 'Gaming Tax (Amendment) Regulations 2026, Legal Notices 84 of 2026 and 86 of 2026, published 1 April 2026'.
defects.correction: Unverifiable. legislation.mt shows S.L. 583.10 (Gaming Tax Regulations) with a point-in-time of 24/06/2022 and no 2026 amendment surfaced; the MGA site returned nothing on a 2026 tax change. The rate structure described is also anomalous: Malta's 5% gaming tax applies flat to revenue from Malta-based players and is not differentiated by licence type, so a split into 10% for Types 2-4 and 15% for Type 1 looks constructed rather than reported. The brief hedges only 'SECONDARY as to the exact LN numbers' while stating the rates and the commencement date as fact, and then lists 'Malta's gaming tax changed on 1 October 2026' in the risks — a date that is still in the future as of 14 September 2026.

defects.claim: 'Spain expressly has NO pure-skill exemption' — Art. 3(a) Ley 13/2011 catches money risked on uncertain outcomes 'con independencia de que predomine... el grado de habilidad'. Authority cited as 'Arts. 1, 2, 3, 9'.
defects.correction: Two problems. (1) Art. 3(a) (BOE consolidated text) requires the uncertain future results to be 'dependientes **en alguna medida del azar**' — dependent to some degree on chance. The 'independencia de que predomine la habilidad' clause means skill-predominance is no defence *once a chance element is present*; it does not capture a contest with no chance element at all. 'No pure-skill exemption' overstates this. (2) The general-licence categories (apuestas, rifas, concursos, otros juegos) sit in **Article 10**, not Article 9, and 'concursos' is defined at Art. 3(e) as offers made through media (TV/radio/internet) requiring an economic outlay with prizes determined by chance, competition or knowledge tests — a definition whose fit with an app-based duel the brief never tests.

defects.claim: France: Model C is 'flatly prohibited'; 'the first [sentence of L320-1] kills Model C'; France is 'THE CLEAREST NO IN THE EU, AND IT IS SPECIFICALLY A NO TO SKILL GAMES'.
defects.correction: By the brief's own quoted text, L320-1 CSI catches operations offered to the public 'pour faire naître l'espérance d'un gain qui serait dû, **même partiellement, au hasard**' where a financial sacrifice is required. Chance remains a constituent element. The 'savoir-faire' sentence closes the skill-predominance escape for mixed games; it does not prohibit paid-entry contests decided wholly by knowledge or ability, which continue lawfully in France (paid chess and bridge tournaments, quiz competitions, jeux-concours). The correct statement is that France catches any contest with *any* chance element — which on the brief's own facts (randomly drawn questions, reflex timers) probably does catch FACT//DUEL — not that France prohibits skill games as a class. The brief also concedes the L320-1 wording was never fetched from Legifrance (403), so the quotation itself rests on a search snippet; I was likewise unable to fetch Legifrance to confirm it.

defects.claim: 'No EU member state uses that [consideration] gateway' — so the free-alternative-method-of-entry structure has no EU counterpart and Model B is structurally unlaunchable EU-wide.
defects.correction: Every EU definition the brief itself quotes turns on a stake/payment limb, which is the functional analogue of consideration: Germany's § 3(1) GlüStV asks whether an *Entgelt* is demanded; and Spellagen 3 kap. 4 § expressly provides that 'licens krävs inte för spel där deltagande inte kräver betalning av en insats' — no licence is required for games where participation requires no stake. The brief's own Sweden entry lists 'free-to-enter games' as a statutory exemption, contradicting the blanket claim. The defensible narrow point is that no EU state accepts a *dual* paid-plus-free entry route as cleansing the paid route (France pre-empts it in terms). Stating it as 'no consideration gateway exists' is wrong and invites the founder to dismiss free-entry designs that may in fact work in specific states.

defects.claim: Model A verdict: 'lawful — No gambling licence is needed in any member state.'
defects.correction: Self-contradicted within the same entry: condition (2) states that if coins buy randomised rewards, the Belgian Gaming Commission's 2018 position makes it illegal gambling — 'this is the one place Model A can become criminal' — and the risks section repeats it. A verdict of 'lawful in any member state' cannot coexist with a stated criminal exposure in Belgium. The verdict should be conditional, not flat. Separately, the brief calls the Belgian item a 'ruling'; the 2018 output of the Kansspelcommissie was a research report/position paper on loot boxes, not a formal adjudicative ruling, and the brief itself marks the ruling text UNVERIFIED.

defects.claim: Subdivision status labels: Austria 'prohibited'; Sweden 'licence-required'.
defects.correction: Both labels contradict the brief's own model analysis. Austria is labelled 'prohibited' while its detail says 'Model C: outside gambling law — GSpG § 1(1) captures only games where the outcome depends exclusively or predominantly on chance', and the Model C section puts Austria in Camp 1. Sweden is labelled 'licence-required' while the headline and Camp 1 put Sweden outside gambling law. A founder or engineer reading the subdivision table for geo-blocking decisions gets the opposite instruction from the one the narrative gives. The brief also concedes GSpG § 1(1) text was never fetched.

defects.claim: Netherlands: 'Dutch courts have gone both ways on borderline cases (the Hoge Raad held poker to be a game of chance in 1998; the Hague District Court reached the opposite view in 2010), so this is not a safe harbour to assume.'
defects.correction: Presenting the 2010 Rechtbank 's-Gravenhage decision as live counter-authority is misleading: it was reversed on appeal by the Gerechtshof Den Haag and Dutch higher courts have consistently maintained that poker is a kansspel under the Wok. The honest framing is that the Dutch 'overwegende invloed' test has been applied *against* skill claims at appellate level, which makes the Netherlands materially less favourable for Model C than the brief's Camp 1 placement implies — not a live 50/50. The brief also concedes the Wok Art. 1(1)(a) text was never fetched from the statute.

defects.claim: Malta: 'FOR MODEL B/DUELS the likelier fit is Type 3: games of chance not played against the house.'
defects.correction: Internally inconsistent with the brief's own skill argument. Type 3 is, on the brief's own quoted MGA definition, a class of **games of chance**. Recommending Type 3 for a knowledge duel requires conceding the product is a game of chance — which destroys the Camp 1 analysis in Germany/Austria/Netherlands/Sweden and strengthens capture in Denmark, Spain, Ireland and Italy. The brief presents Type 3 and Type 4 as interchangeable fallbacks without flagging that choosing Type 3 is a characterisation with EU-wide consequences. The reg. 8 Gaming Authorisations Regulations cross-reference for controlled skill games could not be verified from the primary text (legislation.mt served only metadata).

defects.claim: Risks section: 'Malta's gaming tax changed on 1 October 2026; ... the Netherlands re-licenses its 2021 cohort on 1 October 2026.'
defects.correction: Both are stated in the past/completed tense for dates that have not occurred — today is 14 September 2026. Combined with the fact that neither event could be independently confirmed, a reader will treat two future, unconfirmed events as accomplished facts when budgeting and sequencing.

defects.claim: Austria reform: 'notified to the European Commission in August 2026 (three-month standstill)', 'reportedly 20-30 licences', 'unlicensed operators serving Austrians must stop by 1 January 2027 or face an 18-month licensing exclusion (rising to 24 months from 2030)', consultation closing 15 July 2026.
defects.correction: Unverifiable. The Commission's TRIS notification database would not return Austrian 2026 notifications to me, and no primary source confirms any element of this. The 18-month-rising-to-24-months-from-2030 exclusion is an unusually specific claim to rest on law-firm and trade reporting. The brief also omits the directly relevant hard fact that Österreichische Lotterien's existing electronic-lotteries concession has a fixed expiry, which is what actually drives the reform timetable. Verify against the TRIS notification number before geo-blocking or exit decisions are made on the 1 January 2027 date.

defects.claim: Romania: 'From 1 August 2025 the authorisation tax on online gambling rose from 21% to 30% of gambling revenues and the minimum annual authorisation tax rose to EUR 480,000.' Latvia: 'the Lotteries and Gambling Supervisory Inspection (IAUI) was abolished on 1 April 2026 and its functions transferred to the State Revenue Service (VID).'
defects.correction: Neither figure nor the Latvian transfer date could be confirmed against any primary source. The Romanian rate is reported elsewhere at figures other than 30%, and the EUR 480,000 minimum is the single number the brief uses to disqualify an entire market ('disqualifies Romania for an early-stage product regardless of the legal analysis') — a decision-grade number resting entirely on secondary reporting. Both are flagged SECONDARY in the brief, but both are then used operationally. Verify ONJN orders and the Latvian gambling law amendment before relying.

defects.claim: Italy: 'ADM awarded 52 concessions to 46 operators in September 2025, each operator capped at 5 concessions'; Italy listed as a licensable Model C market.
defects.correction: The concession counts are unverified. More importantly, the brief marks the Italian cost as 'UNVERIFIED' while recommending Italy as one of the five markets where Model C is licensable — omitting that D.Lgs. 41/2024 sets a multi-million-euro concession fee per remote concession (widely reported at around EUR 7m for a nine-year concession) and that Italy operates a near-total gambling advertising ban under the Decreto Dignità. Either fact alone removes Italy from an early-stage founder's realistic footprint. A checklist that lists Italy as an action item with cost 'UNVERIFIED' materially understates the barrier.

defects.claim: 'the Digital Fairness Act is on the Commission's work programme for Q4 2026 with virtual currencies and loot boxes expressly in scope' (stated in Model A, Model D and the checklist).
defects.correction: The Commission work programme slot for the Digital Fairness Act has been indicated as Q3 2026 rather than Q4 2026 in the Commission's own programming documents. The brief flags the item SECONDARY but repeats the Q4 date three times. Given today's date (14 September 2026) the distinction matters: if the proposal landed in Q3 it already exists in draft and should be read, not awaited.

defects.claim: Ireland: 'Commencement order signed 3 February 2026, effective 5 February 2026; remote betting applications opened 9 February 2026; remote betting licence requirement bit from 1 July 2026; in-person from 1 December 2026'; exemptions for 'one-off charitable lotteries with prizes under €2,000, and marketing lotteries with a €5,000 prize limit'.
defects.correction: None of these dates or thresholds could be verified — irishstatutebook.ie, oireachtas.ie and grai.ie all refused the fetch (403), and the brief concedes the same. The Act's section 2 definitions, which the entire Irish verdict turns on, are quoted only through a law-firm guide. Ireland is described as 'THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL NEW REGIME FOR THIS PRODUCT'; a verdict of that weight resting wholly on secondary restatement of statutory definitions, with a six-date commencement timeline none of which is primary-sourced, should be treated as provisional.

missing: Germany § 33d GewO: the permit requirement for commercially operating 'andere Spiele mit Gewinnmöglichkeit' — games with a chance to win that are NOT Glücksspiel. This is exactly the category a paid skill contest falls into when it escapes § 3(1) GlüStV, and it is the direct answer to the brief's advice to 'run Model C in Germany unlicensed'. Not mentioned anywhere in the document.

Payments and e-money authorisation. Every model with a cash-out (B, and C where prizes are money) requires holding and remitting player funds. That triggers PSD2/EMD2 authorisation or a regulated PSP/e-money partner, plus player-fund segregation obligations that are licence conditions in DK, NL, SE, ES and MT. The brief covers AML in detail and says nothing about payments licensing — a founder could build the whole stack and be unable to move money.

Real licence-cost floors in the markets the brief recommends. Italy's per-concession fee under D.Lgs. 41/2024 (reported around EUR 7m), Greece's fixed licence fees, Portugal's, Czechia's bank guarantee requirements. The checklist marks cost 'UNVERIFIED' for Germany, Spain, Italy, Netherlands, Ireland and Denmark simultaneously — so the document recommends a licensing strategy while disclosing no realistic cost for any of the markets in it except Malta.

Advertising and marketing restrictions. Italy's near-total gambling advertising ban (Decreto Dignità), Spain's Real Decreto 958/2020 restrictions, the Netherlands' untargeted-advertising ban, Belgium's 2023-24 advertising prohibition, Germany's advertising limits. A licensed Model C in these markets could be legal to operate and impossible to market — decisive for a consumer app and entirely absent.

Local establishment / local representative requirements: Slovakia's registered representative is mentioned, but the equivalent requirements in Poland (Polish seat or office — mentioned only in passing), Hungary, Czechia, Greece and Romania are not, nor is the general point that several regimes require an EEA-established entity with local tax registration before an application is even accepted.

Player-winnings withholding tax and gambling VAT treatment (Spain, Romania, Greece, Portugal). These change prize-pool economics and require product changes at the payout layer, not just a finance line item.

Prize-competition and promotional-game regimes that sit OUTSIDE gambling law but still bite: the Dutch Gedragscode promotionele kansspelen, Austrian Preisausschreiben rules, and national unfair-commercial-practice rules on paid entry contests. The brief's Camp 1 states are described as having no applicable regime at all once gambling law is escaped, which is not true of any of them.

Age verification and minor-protection duties that apply to Models A and D independently of gambling law (German JuSchG, the DSA's minor-protection provisions, national youth-media law). The brief says of Model D 'No gambling-law authority is engaged' and stops there.

What happens to the rake. The brief never analyses whether FACT//DUEL takes a commission from a player-funded pot (which is what makes it Type 3 P2P in Malta and a 'stake' in most definitions) versus paying a fixed announced prize pool from its own funds (which in several states removes the stake limb entirely). This is a bigger structural lever than the timer length the brief calls 'the single highest-leverage design variable', and it is the difference between licensable and out-of-scope in Germany, Austria and the Netherlands.

A stated method and date-of-check for each subdivision. Roughly half the 27 entries carry 'UNVERIFIED' statute citations with no article numbers, and several (Bulgaria, Croatia, Estonia, Hungary, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia) rest on a single '2026 gambling regulators directory'. The document does not tell the reader which entries were checked against primary law (Denmark, Spain, Sweden, the Commission page and the AMLR were) and which are directory-derived, so all 27 read with equal apparent authority.

defects.claim: HEADLINE: "the cliff edge is REDEEMABILITY, not staking: the moment a purchased coin balance can be turned back into money you are presumptively issuing electronic money (Directive 2009/110/EC Art 2(2))".
defects.correction: EMD2 Art 2(2) contains no redeemability limb. Its two elements are (i) stored monetary value representing a claim on the issuer, issued on receipt of funds for the purpose of making payment transactions, and (ii) acceptance by a natural or legal person OTHER THAN the issuer. Redemption at par is Art 11 — an obligation that follows from already being an e-money issuer, not a trigger that creates one. The brief's own authority contradicts it: EBA Q&A 2022_6336 (Final, published 17/01/2025, citing CJEU C-661/22) states acceptance requires "the transferability and voluntary acceptance of electronic money as a separate monetary asset, and not simply as the reception by the payee of funds resulting from redeemed e-money" — i.e. a network of third parties who accept the instrument itself. A strictly closed-loop coin that the issuer alone redeems, to the same customer, fails limb (ii) however redeemable it is. The correct cliff edge is THIRD-PARTY ACCEPTANCE / TRANSFERABILITY, with redeemability as strong evidence of a payment purpose under limb (i), not as a presumption. The brief half-concedes this inside Model B and then contradicts itself in the headline.

defects.claim: RISK REGISTER: "A 'goodwill cash refund' policy for unhappy players ... or an account-closure policy that returns the unspent balance as money — any one of these can start to satisfy the second limb of EMD2 Art 2(2)."
defects.correction: The second limb is acceptance by a person other than the issuer. A refund paid by the issuer back to its own customer involves no third party accepting the coin at all, so it cannot satisfy that limb — nor can returning an unspent balance on account closure, nor the statutory CRD withdrawal refund the brief itself mandates elsewhere. Only the player-to-player transfer / grey-market example in that same sentence is a genuine limb-(ii) risk. As written, this instructs the founder to avoid lawful consumer-friendly refund practices on a mistaken legal basis, while under-weighting the feature (transferability) that actually matters.

defects.claim: "AMLR Art 2(1)(12) gives the FIRST EU-WIDE definition of 'gambling service' ... Because it is a regulation, it applies directly in all 27 member states without transposition — no more forum-shopping the definition."
defects.correction: Not the first. Directive (EU) 2015/849 (AMLD4) Art 3(14) already defines gambling services in materially identical words — verified verbatim: "'gambling services' means a service which involves wagering a stake with monetary value in games of chance, including those with an element of skill such as lotteries, casino games, poker games and betting transactions that are provided at a physical location, or by any means at a distance, by electronic means or any other technology for facilitating communication, and at the individual request of a recipient of services". That definition has been EU law since 2015 (transposition 26 June 2017), and AMLD4 Art 2(1)(3)(f) has made "providers of gambling services" obliged entities EU-wide ever since. The AMLR carries the wording across into a regulation; it does not invent it.

defects.claim: CHECKLIST: "Build AML/CFT capability for a 10 July 2027 start date if you pursue Model B or C" / Model B: "From 10 July 2027, Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) applies directly and makes providers of 'gambling services' obliged entities."
defects.correction: This is the most dangerous framing in the brief. AML obligations for gambling service providers are already live across the EU under national transpositions of AMLD4/AMLD5 (Directive (EU) 2015/849 Art 2(1)(3)(f), definition at Art 3(14)) — customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, FIU reporting and registration/licensing with the national AML supervisor. 10 July 2027 is the date the directly-applicable regulation replaces that regime, not the date AML first bites. A founder reading this checklist could launch Model B in late 2026 with no AML programme and be operating unlawfully in most Member States on day one. The checklist should read "comply with national AML law NOW; re-paper to AMLR by 10 July 2027."

defects.claim: "Because it is a regulation, it applies directly in all 27 member states without transposition — no more forum-shopping the definition." (AMLR gambling scope)
defects.correction: National discretion survives. AMLD4 Art 2(2) expressly permits Member States, other than for casinos and following a risk assessment, to "exempt, in full or in part, providers of certain gambling services" on the basis of proven low risk, with notification to the Commission — and the AML package preserves an equivalent low-risk exemption option. So whether a given paid-entry skill contest is an AML obliged entity remains a per-market answer even after 10 July 2027. The brief omits the exemption route entirely, which also happens to be the most plausible escape hatch for Model C.

defects.claim: CHECKLIST (DSA baseline): "Baseline duties that apply to ALL intermediary services regardless of size (Art 19 does not exempt these): Art 11 ... Art 12 ... Art 14 ... Art 16 ... Art 15 transparency reporting also applies to hosting services."
defects.correction: Wrong for this company. DSA Art 15(2) reads: "Paragraph 1 of this Article shall not apply to providers of intermediary services that qualify as micro or small enterprises as defined in Recommendation 2003/361/EC and which are not very large online platforms within the meaning of Article 33 of this Regulation." The brief elsewhere assumes micro/small status (it relies on Art 19 for exactly that). Art 15 transparency reporting therefore does NOT apply. Arts 11, 12, 14 and 16 do. Listing Art 15 among the size-blind baseline is a straightforward misstatement that would generate unnecessary annual reporting work.

defects.claim: MODEL C: "What is SETTLED: (a) the entry fee is consideration for an electronically supplied service, VAT-able at the consumer's rate through OSS (C-472/24 logic applies a fortiori to a fee, and Art 58 VAT Directive is unambiguous)."
defects.correction: Not settled, and the brief cites the wrong exemption. It tests Model C only against Art 135(1)(e) (currency transactions). The relevant provision is Art 135(1)(i) VAT Directive, which exempts "betting, lotteries and other forms of gambling, subject to the conditions and limitations laid down by each Member State." If a Member State characterises the paid-entry timed duel as gambling — precisely the question the brief itself calls unresolved three sentences later — the entry fee may be VAT-EXEMPT in that state and outside the OSS return, with knock-on input-VAT recovery consequences. The brief cannot label the gambling characterisation "unsettled" for AMLR and "settled" for VAT when the same characterisation drives both. Related: for any Model B/C wagering leg, the Glawe line (C-38/93; C-377/11 International Bingo) can make the taxable amount the operator's margin rather than gross stakes — also absent.

defects.claim: "CJEU C-472/24 MB 'Žaidimų valiuta', judgment 5 March 2026 ... settled that selling in-game virtual currency for real money is a taxable electronically supplied service ... VAT is due on the FULL consideration (Art 73) at the moment the coins are sold" and headline "VAT on coin sales from the first euro (CJEU C-472/24 ...)".
defects.correction: The case and date are real (Lithuanian reference; judgment 5 March 2026 — the brief's own flagged date is the right one) but the facts are misdescribed and the holding over-extended. The taxable person was MB "Žaidimų valiuta", a THIRD-PARTY TRADER reselling RuneScape Gold on a secondary market, not a publisher issuing its own currency. The Court held that exchanging real currency for units usable only inside an online game is not exempt under Art 135(1)(e) and is not a "voucher" under Art 30a, so Art 73 general rules apply. Extending that to a first-party issuer's own coin sale is a reasonable inference, not a holding — and the single-purpose voucher analysis (Art 30a(2)) for a first-party issuer was not before the Court. Separately, "VAT from the first euro" for a non-EU seller follows from Art 58 plus the fact that the Art 59c EUR 10,000 threshold is confined to EU-established sellers; it has nothing to do with C-472/24.

defects.claim: HEADLINE: "everything up to that line (Models A, C, D) is lawful but carries four non-negotiable EU obligations" — listing the 14-day unspent-coin refund right and real-money price labelling among them; Model A: "Four hard obligations attach the instant you take the first euro."
defects.correction: Two of the four rest wholly on the CPC Key Principles, which the document itself disclaims in footnote 1: "The present document does therefore by no means bind the national authorities or the European Commission. Solely the competent authorities and courts can finally decide on the legality of commercial practices", and non-compliance is not necessarily unlawful. The "virtual currency is not digital content" premise behind the unspent-coin refund right is a CPC legal theory that Video Games Europe/EGDF dispute and that German courts have gone the other way on. The brief discloses all of this correctly in its risks section — but a founder who reads only the headline and the Model A verdict is told soft law is "non-negotiable" and "hard". Label them enforcement posture, not obligations.

defects.claim: "the AI Omnibus was adopted by Council 29 June 2026, published in the OJ 24 July 2026 and entered into force 27 July 2026."
defects.correction: Uncorroborated precision. The brief's own cited source (Gibson Dunn) records political agreement on 6 May 2026, Council confirmation on 13 May 2026, and formal adoption plus OJ publication only as "expected before 2 August 2026". No reachable source records a 29 June Council adoption, a 24 July OJ publication, or a 27 July entry into force — and a three-day interval between OJ publication and entry into force is atypical. The SUBSTANCE does check out: Annex III stand-alone high-risk deferred to 2 December 2027, Annex I embedded high-risk to 2 August 2028, Art 5 prohibitions not deferred and in force since 2 February 2025. Also omitted: Art 50 transparency obligations remain live from 2 August 2026, and a new Art 5 prohibition (nudifiers/CSAM) was added with a transitional period to 2 December 2026.

defects.claim: "Latombe appealed on 31 October 2025 and the appeal is pending before the CJEU as Case C-703/25 P ... with no hearing date announced as at mid-2026 and Microsoft granted leave to intervene for the Commission on 29 June 2026."
defects.correction: The General Court dismissal on 3 September 2025 and the appeal lodged 31 October 2025 are corroborated (WilmerHale). The case number "C-703/25 P" and the "Microsoft granted leave to intervene ... on 29 June 2026" detail are corroborated by nothing reachable — neither the IAPP nor the WilmerHale piece the brief cites mentions either, and CURIA was unretrievable. Do not repeat the case number or the intervention date without checking the CURIA register. The underlying advice (DPF valid today, appeal live, keep SCCs plus a TIA as fallback) is sound.

defects.claim: "European Commission age-verification blueprint / 'mini-wallet' (v1 14 July 2025, declared feature-ready 15 April 2026)" and "the Commission declared the blueprint feature-ready on 15 April 2026".
defects.correction: No such declaration is traceable. The Commission's own digital-strategy release of 10 October 2025 (an enhanced SECOND version — which the brief does not mention) describes the blueprint as "now being thoroughly pilot tested", says "the first customised apps are expected to be published early 2026", and nowhere uses "feature-ready". Version 1 in July 2025 and the five pilot states (Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, Spain) do check out.

defects.claim: PSD3/PSR: "final compromise texts published 23 April 2026, NOT yet adopted ... (expected H2 2026), with most substantive rules applying roughly 21 months after entry into force — realistically late 2027/2028."
defects.correction: The brief's own cited source (Norton Rose Fulbright) says the PSR applies 18 months after entry into force, with only the payee-name/identifier verification duty at 24 months, and puts expected OJ publication at end of Q2 2026, not H2 2026. The 27 November 2025 provisional agreement checks out; the "23 April 2026 final compromise texts" date does not appear in any reachable source. Also omitted and material to Model B: PSD3 REPEALS EMD2 outright and existing EMI authorisations survive only 24 months after entry into force (extendable to 30), with a mandatory re-application — so an EMI licence obtained for Model B in 2027 would need re-papering almost immediately.

missing: Directive (EU) 2019/770 (Digital Content Directive) is never cited anywhere in the brief, despite being the core contract-law instrument for exactly this product. Art 19 DCD governs when a trader may modify digital content or a digital service during a continuous supply — that, not UCTD Art 3 alone, is what constrains the post-launch coin rebalancing the brief warns about, and it carries a free termination right for the consumer where the modification adversely affects access or use. Arts 14–18 govern conformity remedies, price reduction and reimbursement on termination. The "legal guarantee of conformity for digital content and services" that CPC Principle 4 requires you to disclose pre-contractually comes from this directive. Its absence is the single largest gap in the brief's consumer-law layer.

European Accessibility Act, Directive (EU) 2019/882 — requirements have APPLIED since 28 June 2025 and expressly cover e-commerce and consumer-facing digital services (websites and mobile apps used to conclude consumer contracts). Microenterprises providing services are exempt (Art 4(5)), which is why the brief can ignore it today — but the exemption evaporates at 10 staff or EUR 2m turnover, and retrofitting WCAG-level accessibility into a heavily animated, timer-driven, juice-and-ceremony game UI after launch is expensive. Enforced by national market surveillance authorities with fines. Not mentioned once.

The conflict-of-laws hook is missing. The brief asserts throughout that CRD, UCPD, UCTD and (implicitly) DCD bind a non-EU-established trader without explaining WHY: Rome I Regulation (EC) No 593/2008 Art 6(1)–(2) applies the mandatory consumer-protection law of the consumer's habitual residence to a trader who directs activities to that Member State, and a choice-of-law clause cannot deprive the consumer of it; Brussels Ia Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 Art 18 lets the consumer sue at home. A founder given a US- or offshore-law ToS template may believe a governing-law clause solves this. It does not, and nothing in the brief says so.

VAT Directive Art 135(1)(i) — the gambling exemption ("betting, lotteries and other forms of gambling, subject to the conditions and limitations laid down by each Member State") — is never mentioned, though it is the exemption that actually matters for Models B and C. Nor is the Glawe line (C-38/93 Glawe; C-377/11 International Bingo Technology) on the taxable amount for wagering being the operator's retained margin rather than gross stakes. Both materially change the VAT model for any money-play variant.

Directive (EU) 2020/1828 on representative actions (applicable 25 June 2023) — qualified entities can bring collective redress across the EU for infringements of the CRD, UCPD, UCTD, DCD, GDPR and the VAT-adjacent consumer rules. For a coin economy aimed at a population containing minors this is the realistic enforcement vector alongside CPC action, and the brief's risk register never mentions consumer class actions at all.

Geo-blocking Regulation (EU) 2018/302 Art 4 — the brief advises "either absorb the spread or vary the price per country" to handle differing VAT rates, without flagging that differentiating general conditions of access to an electronically supplied service by the customer's nationality, residence or place of establishment is constrained by this Regulation. There is room to price differently per market, but the implementation detail (how you determine and enforce the country) is exactly where geo-blocking complaints arise, and the brief gives the advice with no caveat.

Directive 2000/31/EC (e-Commerce Directive) Arts 5, 6 and 10 — baseline information-society-service provider identification duties (name, geographic address, contact details, trade register, and the commercial-communication identification rules), which sit alongside CRD Art 6 and apply independently of it. Also absent is the point that the country-of-origin principle in Art 3 offers a non-EU-established provider nothing.

CRD Art 8(2) (the "order with obligation to pay" button labelling) is applied only to Model D's subscription confirm button. It applies equally to every coin-purchase button in Models A, B and C, and failure to comply means the consumer is not bound by the contract at all — a direct revenue-reversal risk, not a paperwork one.

The AMLR/AMLD customer due diligence trigger for gambling — collection of winnings, wagering a stake, or both, amounting to EUR 2,000 or more in a single or linked transactions — is recorded as "UNVERIFIED" rather than researched, even though it is the number that determines whether Model B/C needs full KYC at first deposit or only above a threshold. It is the most operationally load-bearing unknown left open in the whole brief.

defects.claim: "s.2(1)(j) counts purchased, non-cashable virtual coins as a 'stake'" and "CASH-OUT IS NOT REQUIRED for this to be an offence" — presented as the headline and as "THE DECISIVE RISK", with the escrow duel said to "flip from lawful to criminal" the instant coins become purchasable.
defects.correction: This is the brief's central conclusion and it is genuinely unsettled, not settled. The brief's OWN cited source (respawn.outlookindia.com, 'Pocket casinos: how mobile games are exposing PROGA's loopholes') states the contrary reading is the prevailing one: a game 'which takes real money and returns dice rolls and stickers, almost certainly falls within PROGA's definition of an online social game', reasoning that in-game currency with no cash-out value is not 'monetary gain'. The brief cites that article only for the softer proposition that commentary calls it a 'loophole', and suppresses that it reaches the opposite legal verdict on the precise fact pattern. The brief's own 'uncertain' section further concedes the construction is 'a genuine ambiguity' with no determination or judgment resolving it, and that the chapeau 'recognised as equivalent or convertible to money' protects non-convertible coins. A verdict flagged internally as ambiguous cannot be the headline's flat criminal finding. Correct framing: purchased-but-non-cashable coin staking is an untested and contested position on which reasonable Indian counsel currently differ, with the weight of published 2026 commentary on the permissive side.

defects.claim: s.2(1)(j) is read one way for purchased coins (purchase alone makes them 'other stakes') and the opposite way for free points ("the definition requires the item to be BOTH 'recognised as equivalent or convertible to money' AND 'purchased by paying money directly or by indirect means'").
defects.correction: These two readings are mutually exclusive and the brief relies on each where it produces the more alarming or more convenient answer. Model A's reasoning and the 'DECISIVE RISK' entry treat 'includes credits, coins, token or objects ... which is purchased' as a self-sufficient inclusive limb; the Expeditions checklist item expressly states the definition is conjunctive. On the conjunctive reading the brief itself endorses, purchased coins that are non-transferable, non-redeemable and have no external market are NOT 'other stakes', because they are not 'recognised as equivalent or convertible to money' — which destroys the headline. The brief must pick one construction and follow it through both conclusions.

defects.claim: The 'expectation of winning' limb of s.2(1)(g) is "satisfied both by cash redemption and by winning further stakes".
defects.correction: The verified text (confirmed verbatim against Bar & Bench's quotation) reads 'in expectation of winning which entails monetary AND other enrichment in return of money or other stakes'. The conjunction is 'and', not 'or'. There is a serious argument that monetary enrichment is a necessary component and that winning further non-monetary in-game credit alone does not satisfy the limb — which is exactly the reading the Outlook/Respawn analysis adopts. The brief never mentions the conjunction, let alone argues around it, while relying on the disjunctive reading to criminalise Model B and the duel mechanic.

defects.claim: "The 2026 amendment ... adds a Grievance Appellate Committee route with a 30-day user appeal window" (IT Rules checklist item).
defects.correction: The Grievance Appellate Committee and the 30-day user appeal window were created by the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2022 (rule 3A), in force since October 2022 — not by the 2026 amendment. The 2026 amendment (notified 10 Feb 2026, effective 20 Feb 2026) is confirmed to cover the 3-hour takedown for contempt/defamation-type categories, quarterly user notification, and synthetically-generated-content labelling/metadata duties; the GAC is not among its innovations. A founder told the appeal route is new in 2026 will mis-date their compliance baseline by four years.

defects.claim: "The final Rules ... dropped the Grievance Appellate Committee tier" (uncertain section, used to justify the Rules' restructuring narrative).
defects.correction: Multiple sources the brief itself cites describe an appellate tier surviving in the final 2026 Rules: Mondaq reports '30-day timelines for Authority and Appellate Authority decisions', and Bar & Bench reports an appeal timeline of '30 days to file; 30 days for disposal'. The claim that the appellate tier was dropped is contradicted by the brief's own source set, and it matters because it is the only route a founder has if an adverse determination lands.

defects.claim: "OGAI cannot make an e-sport determination without the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports member present and concurring" (Model C reasoning and checklist).
defects.correction: No source supports a member-specific concurrence requirement. The 2026 Rules' decision-making provisions as reported by SCC Online are ordinary: quorum of at least 50% of total members, majority vote, Chairperson's casting vote in ties, with urgent decisions permitted by written order notified to members within 3 days. OGAI is described as an ex officio body that includes a Joint Secretary from Youth Affairs & Sports among six members — membership is not the same as a veto or a concurrence condition. Treat 'present and concurring' as unverified and probably invented.

defects.claim: "Reserve Bank of India (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025, dated 15 September 2025" creating three categories with an "Outward Collection Account" for Indians paying a foreign merchant, per-transaction cap ₹25 lakh.
defects.correction: Two problems. (1) The instrument title could not be confirmed on RBI's own Master Directions or notifications pages; the RBI framework is titled 'Reserve Bank of India (Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025' — the inserted words 'Regulation of' are not part of any title I could verify, and neither was the 15 September 2025 date. (2) 'Outward Collection Account' does not appear to be RBI terminology. The PA-CB framework uses the Import Collection Account (ICA) for the leg where Indian buyers pay foreign merchants, and the Export Collection Account (ECA) for the reverse. The ₹25 lakh figure derives from the October 2023 PA-CB circular's per-unit import cap and its survival into the 2025 consolidation is unverified. Do not plan payment architecture against these labels or that cap.

defects.claim: "DPDP Rules 2025, G.S.R. 846(E), 13 November 2025" cited three times as a precise gazette reference.
defects.correction: The G.S.R. number could not be corroborated from any source reached, and the date is contested — Wikipedia's entry for the DPDP Rules gives 14 November 2025 for notification. Given that the brief expressly flags the 2026 Gaming Rules G.S.R. as unverified, quoting a bare G.S.R. number for the DPDP Rules with no equivalent caveat is inconsistent and is exactly the fabricated-citation failure mode. Verify G.S.R. 846(E) against the gazette before it appears in anything a regulator or investor reads.

defects.claim: DPDP s.9(3) is "an absolute bar, not a consent-waivable one" on tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children.
defects.correction: Correct that it cannot be cured by consent, but not absolute. s.9(4) empowers the Central Government to exempt classes of data fiduciaries, or processing for prescribed purposes, from both s.9(1) and s.9(3), and the DPDP Rules 2025 exercise that power (Fourth Schedule). The exemptions are unlikely to reach a quiz game, but describing the bar as absolute misstates the statutory architecture and will mislead anyone testing whether a narrow exemption is available.

defects.claim: "The cheapest compliant answer is a genuine 18+ gate for India."
defects.correction: An 18+ gate is not a DPDP exit. The DPDP Rules 2025 require a data fiduciary to exercise due diligence to verify that a user claiming to be an adult is in fact not a child — a self-declaration checkbox is not that, and it is the reason the Rules prescribe DigiLocker/virtual-token-based verification at all. Separately, the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026 impose age verification on online social games in their own right (see omissions), so an 18+ gate creates a verification obligation rather than removing one. And DPDP applies in full to adult users regardless.

defects.claim: "s.14 lets blocking notwithstanding s.69A of the IT Act 2000."
defects.correction: Unverified, and the framing is doing work. PRS's summary describes the power as empowering the Central Government to block information relating to online money gaming services; whether s.14 overrides s.69A or instead operates through the s.69A procedure and the 2009 Blocking Rules is a material difference — it determines whether the s.69A procedural safeguards (committee, hearing, reasoned order, confidentiality) apply to a blocking order against the founder's app. The brief asserts the override without quoting the provision.

defects.claim: Rule numbers of the 2026 Rules are treated as reliable throughout the checklist ("classified by OGAI under rule 9", "evidential before OGAI under rule 9", "rule 10(2)", "rule 11", "rules 12-14") with the unverified caveat buried in a separate section.
defects.correction: The brief's own sources conflict. Legal500 and gaganlegal place the five-factor determination test at rule 9 (gaganlegal: rule 8 determination, rule 9 factors, rule 10 procedure, rule 11 validity, rule 12 registration, rule 13 e-sports, rule 14 certificate validity), but Bar & Bench assigns rule 9 to permissible e-sports payments and places mandatory e-sports registration at rule 12(1)(b), while ipleaders puts registration across rules 12-19 and grievance in Part V. The numbering is probably right on the balance of sources, but the checklist repeats it as an issuer/authority citation without any inline flag, which is how an indicative number becomes a quoted authority in a founder's board pack.

missing: USER-SAFETY DUTIES ON THE LAWFUL MODELS. The 2026 Rules impose age verification, parental controls, time limits, fair-play monitoring and grievance redressal on online social games generally — i.e. on Models A and D, the two the brief calls lawful — not only on money games or registered games. The checklist contains none of these as an operative item; 'rule 23 safety disclosure' appears only inside the 'uncertain' list, and a grievance mechanism appears only as a document to attach to a voluntary determination application. A founder working the checklist would ship Model A or D into India believing there are no India-specific gaming obligations at all beyond tax and data.

INDIA DATA LOCALISATION. Providers of registered online social games and e-sports must retain traffic data, metadata and related information on computer resources located in India. The brief recommends filing for voluntary determination/registration as 'the cheapest insurance available' without disclosing that registration is what switches on an India data-residency obligation. That is a direct, unflagged cost consequence of the brief's own recommendation.

PRIZE COMPETITIONS ACT, 1955 AND STATE PRIZE-COMPETITION LAW. The brief declares flatly that 'there is no sweepstakes doctrine, no dual currency carve-out and no alternative method of entry defence anywhere in Indian law'. It never mentions the Prize Competitions Act, 1955, or state prize-competition and lottery legislation, which are the instruments that actually govern free-entry and skill-based prize competitions in India and which constrain any AMOE-style design a US founder would reach for. Saying the doctrine does not exist, rather than saying a different statute governs it badly, leaves the founder unable to evaluate the design space.

THE APPEAL ROUTE. Having wrongly stated that the final Rules dropped the appellate tier, the brief gives no appeal path at all against an adverse OGAI determination, cessation direction or blocking order — despite its own risks section saying enforcement is 'fast and intermediary-led', with 'the appeal happening afterwards'. Sources indicate a 30-day window to file and 30 days for disposal. This is the founder's only remedy and it is missing.

WIND-DOWN AND TRANSITION. s.5 bites immediately and enforcement is by delisting and payment cut-off. The brief gives no guidance on what happens to Indian users' existing coin balances, in-flight duels or subscription entitlements on the day a feature is geo-blocked or an app is pulled — refunds, consumer-protection exposure under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020, and chargeback handling.

THE CURRENT FREE PRODUCT IS NOT UNREGULATED.
