The brief repeatedly characterises the existing free product as 'safe' on the gaming analysis and then treats India obligations as beginning 'at the first rupee'. But the 2026 Rules' social-game safeguards and the DPDP child-data regime attach to a free product with Indian users too. The brief's framing invites the founder to defer all India work until monetisation.

ELIGIBILITY TO FILE. The brief recommends a voluntary determination application to OGAI for a possibly-foreign entity but never establishes whether a provider with no Indian presence can file, what the point-of-contact / India-resident-officer requirement does to that, or what filing costs in exposure — a determination application puts a named foreign operator in front of the regulator with a product the brief itself says is the 'highest-scrutiny design you could ship into India'.

defects.claim: "FACT//DUEL's current live UI already uses 'stake', 'escrow' and 'winner takes the escrow'" — and the risk item: "The current live product already stakes 'coins' into an 'escrow' where 'the winner takes the escrow'. That language is shipped, public at the GitHub Pages URL, and indexable. Underwriters read the live site."
defects.correction: The exact phrase "winner takes the escrow" appears NOWHERE in the repository (grep -rni across the whole tree excluding node_modules returns zero hits). "escrow" appears zero times in app/ and components/ — the entire UI layer — and exists only as an internal server state field in lib/server/room-engine.mjs (r.escrow, r.balances[winner] += r.escrow). "stake" appears in the UI layer only as CSS class names (fd-exp-stake-line, stake-label, fd-exp-stakes). So the quoted "live UI" copy does not exist as user-facing text; what is "shipped" is minified JavaScript identifiers in dist-static/assets/index-BWl9btPX.js. Underwriters do not read minified variable names, and JS identifiers are not "indexable" as page copy. The remedial advice (rename these concepts before filing a merchant application) is still worth taking, but the brief invents a verbatim quotation from the product and materially overstates the urgency and the exposure.

defects.claim: "The trigger is FinCEN guidance FIN-2013-G001 (18 March 2013)" — used as the sole FinCEN authority for the Model A "no money transmission" verdict and the Model B administrator/MSB verdict.
defects.correction: FinCEN issued FIN-2019-G001, "Application of FinCEN's Regulations to Certain Business Models Involving Convertible Virtual Currencies," on 9 May 2019. I extracted the PDF text directly: it states it "consolidates current FinCEN regulations, and related administrative rulings and guidance issued since 2011, and then applies these rules and interpretations to obligations under the BSA as they relate to current and emerging business models." That sweep includes FIN-2013-G001. The 2019 guidance is the current consolidated reference and addresses business models the 2013 guidance does not. The 2013 quotations the brief relies on are accurate verbatim (I confirmed each against the FinCEN page), but building both the Model A clearance and the Model B MSB determination on 2013 guidance while never mentioning the 2019 consolidation is citing superseded authority on the single most consequential legal question in the brief.

defects.claim: "The 300x rule is decisive for a duel game: a $1 stake winning $100 is 100x and falls below it; a $1 stake winning $2,000 does not." Paired with: "regular gambling withholding of 24% applies when winnings minus the wager exceed $5,000."
defects.correction: The 300x test gates REPORTING but does not gate WITHHOLDING for the category a head-to-head pot most likely falls into. The Instructions for Forms W-2G and 5754 (rev. 01/2026) state: "Withhold at the 24% rate if the winnings minus the wager are more than $5,000 and are from: Sweepstakes; Wagering pools; Lotteries...or Sports wagering and other wagering transactions, if the winnings are at least 300 times the amount wagered." The 300x qualifier attaches only to the final clause — it does not apply to sweepstakes, wagering pools or lotteries, consistent with IRC 3402(q)(3). A FACT//DUEL pot where losers' stakes fund the winner's prize is plausibly a "wagering pool." A founder told the 300x rule is "decisive" could conclude no obligation arises on a large low-multiple payout and fail to withhold 24% on proceeds over $5,000 — an unrecoverable liability, since the brief itself notes withholding cannot be clawed back from the user after payment.

defects.claim: "Stripe's own FAQ states it does not support gambling businesses 'regardless of local legality'" — presented as a verbatim quotation in both the checklist and the Model B reasoning.
defects.correction: I fetched support.stripe.com/questions/prohibited-and-restricted-businesses-list-faqs. The FAQ conveys this substance — answering "Internet gambling is legal in my region, so why was my application rejected?" by pointing to processor and financial-partner obligations — but the phrase "regardless of local legality" could not be confirmed as actual text on the page. The adjacent quotation the brief gives from the same FAQ ("games of skill (or chance) with cash prizes, sweepstakes, pay-in auctions") IS verbatim, which makes the unverified one more likely to be a paraphrase dressed as a quote. Do not reproduce it inside quotation marks in anything filed or shown to counsel.

defects.claim: "Apple will host [Model C] under 5.3.1 and 5.3.2 (the developer must sponsor the contest and publish official rules stating Apple is not a sponsor), which is a meaningfully lighter regime than 5.3.4."
defects.correction: This is a confident routing decision on a genuinely unsettled question, and it sits oddly inside a model the brief itself grades "unsettled." Guideline 5.3.3 (verified verbatim) bars IAP-purchased credit or currency "for use in conjunction with real money gaming of any kind," and 5.3.4 governs apps that "offer real money gaming." Apple nowhere defines "real money gaming," and its 5.3.4 examples are illustrative ("e.g. sports betting, poker, casino games, horse racing"), not exhaustive. A paid-entry contest paying cash prizes is readily characterised by a reviewer as real money gaming, which would pull Model C into 5.3.4's free-app, licensed, geo-restricted regime and 5.3.3's IAP bar — the opposite of the "lighter regime" the brief promises. The brief gives Model C a planning assumption where it should give a review-risk range.

defects.claim: "Stripe, Adyen, PayPal, Apple IAP and Google Play Billing all accept this as ordinary digital-goods commerce" (Model A), and the checklist's assertion that Model A is "fully served by mainstream rails."
defects.correction: No Adyen or PayPal line item is cited for virtual currency or stored value anywhere in the brief — the Adyen list is cited only for its gambling and game-of-skill entries, and PayPal only for its gambling AUP. The brief's own Paddle finding proves the category is separately policed: Paddle's AUP (13 April 2026, verified verbatim) prohibits "Virtual currency or stored value, including but not limited to store credit, gift cards, vouchers" outright, killing even Model A. Acquirers commonly carry a distinct stored-value/virtual-currency restriction independent of their gambling lines. Asserting Adyen and PayPal acceptance of a coin-sale model without a cited line repeats exactly the mistake the Paddle finding warns about.

defects.claim: "The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act No. 32 of 2025, assent 22 August 2025)... The Rules were notified 22 April 2026 (Wikipedia, secondary)." Subdivision status: "prohibited," with "no commercial workaround."
defects.correction: The Wikipedia article the brief relies on for the Act number and the Rules date carries an AI-generated-content warning, which the brief does not disclose. That same article states commencement is "TBA — not yet in force" and notes ongoing challenges before India's High Courts and the Supreme Court — neither of which appears anywhere in the brief. The brief's substantive advice (do not attempt an Indian rail for B or C) is conservative and almost certainly right, and the Act's skill-inclusive scope is well corroborated elsewhere. But the brief presents an operative, settled payment-facilitation ban when the commencement status of the relevant sections is unestablished and the statute is under constitutional challenge, and it sources two specific citations to a page flagged as machine-generated.

defects.claim: "Texas: effective 1 Jan 2026; a preliminary injunction was stayed by the Fifth Circuit (Morrison Foerster, Nov 2025) so the law is operative."
defects.correction: The substance is correct — I confirmed via the cited Morrison Foerster piece that the W.D. Tex. injunction was stayed by the Fifth Circuit (on a finding that Texas made "a strong showing of likely success on the merits" and that the district court likely erred in applying strict rather than intermediate scrutiny), and the law is in effect. But the date attribution is chronologically doubtful: the cited URL slug is 251111, i.e. 11 November 2025, while the district court injunction it describes issued in late 2025. A November alert cannot have reported a stay of an injunction granted after it. The brief is also internally inconsistent — it states the stay as settled fact in the checklist while marking "UNVERIFIED: current litigation posture" in the subdivision for the same law.

defects.claim: "Requirements 6.4.3... and 11.6.1... were removed from the SAQ A checklist itself but are named as the techniques by which you demonstrate eligibility."
defects.correction: The PCI SSC FAQ presents 6.4.3/11.6.1 techniques as ONE route, not THE route. Per the cited blog post, a merchant may either deploy those techniques itself or obtain confirmation from its payment processor that the processor's solution includes such protections. The brief's phrasing makes a script-inventory/SRI/CSP programme sound like the only path to SAQ A eligibility when a processor attestation may satisfy it. The same FAQ also limits the new criteria to merchants using embedded payment forms (iframes) — which the brief never says, even though it is recommending precisely that integration pattern.

defects.claim: "Note the historic Guideline 4.7.1 real-money-gaming restriction has been removed and 4.7 now covers mini apps, mini games and emulators — do not rely on stale 4.7 advice."
defects.correction: The second half is right: current 4.7 covers "Mini apps, mini games, streaming games, chatbots, plug-ins, and game emulators," and current 4.7.1 concerns privacy compliance, moderation/reporting mechanisms, and Guideline 3.1 conformity for digital goods. But I could not confirm that a real-money-gaming restriction ever sat at 4.7.1. Apple's real-money gaming and sweepstakes rules have lived at 5.3 for years. The brief warns against "stale 4.7 advice" that may never have existed, which manufactures a false sense that a known trap has been cleared. Harmless operationally, but it is an invented citation history in a document whose stated worst failure mode is invented citations.

missing: UIGEA — 31 U.S.C. 5361-5367 and Regulation GG — is never mentioned. This is the single largest omission. It is the actual US federal statute that compels banks and payment processors to identify and block "restricted transactions" connected to unlawful internet gambling, and it is the reason acquirers refuse this category at all. A payments-layer brief that explains Stripe's and Adyen's category lists but not the federal law driving them leaves the founder thinking the obstacle is commercial risk appetite (negotiable) rather than a coding-and-blocking mandate on the rail itself (not negotiable).

State sweepstakes and prize-promotion registration and bonding. New York and Florida require registration and the posting of a bond for prize promotions above $5,000, with filing deadlines before the promotion opens. This bites Model C and any sweepstakes-tier Model B directly, is cheap to comply with and expensive to miss, and appears nowhere — despite the brief covering far more exotic obligations like escheatment.
FIN-2019-G001 (9 May 2019) as the current consolidated FinCEN CVC authority — see defects. Counsel needs to be pointed at the 2019 guidance, not only the 2013 one.

The EU AMLR application date. The brief correctly refuses to assert article numbers or thresholds it could not fetch, but it omits the sequencing fact a founder actually needs: Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 does not apply immediately, and until it does the member state's existing AMLD transposition governs. Without a date the founder cannot tell whether this is a launch blocker or a 2027 roadmap item.

For Model C, whether a skill-contest licence exists to obtain at all. The brief lists "Gambling or skill-gaming licence in each target market" as the prerequisite for Adyen's waiver and for every specialist acquirer, and calls Adyen "more workable." But in most EU/UK jurisdictions there is no licence category for a pure paid-entry skill contest. If so, the waiver prerequisite is unsatisfiable rather than merely slow, and the "Adyen route" for Model C is illusory — which would change the Model C verdict from "unsettled" to something closer to Model B.

That a full-redirect or fully hosted checkout sits outside the new SAQ A script-attack eligibility criterion entirely. The PCI FAQ limits those criteria to embedded-iframe merchants. Given the brief's own warning that FACT//DUEL is a script-heavy React/three.js app in the Magecart target profile, redirecting to a hosted payment page is the obvious architectural answer and is never offered.

State-by-state skill-versus-chance analysis for paid-entry contests. The brief defers this to "the gambling-law layer," but several US states treat any paid-entry cash-prize contest as illegal gambling regardless of skill predominance. Since acquirer acceptance and UIGEA exposure both turn on underlying legality, this determines the payments outcome and cannot be cleanly walled off into another workstream.

Apple's and Google's actual commission rates. Both are flagged UNVERIFIED, yet for Models A and D — the two models the brief clears for launch — store commission is the single largest cost line in the whole document. Every marginal vendor fee is priced but the dominant one is left blank.

Chargeback and friendly-fraud exposure on coin purchases. Digital goods with instant delivery and no shippable proof draw elevated dispute rates, and card-network monitoring programmes (Visa VDMP / Mastercard Excessive Chargeback) impose fines and can force a merchant off the rail. This is a realistic way Model A — the model graded unconditionally lawful — loses its processor.
